q008.explanation: Protected objects enforce readers-writer mutual exclusion at the language level: `function`s run concurrently, while `procedure`s and `entry`s have exclusive access.

q009.explanation: Entry barriers (`when Condition`) provide condition-variable-like waiting without manual lock/unlock or spurious wakeup bugs.

q010.explanation: Synchronous rendezvous combines communication and synchronization in a single construct.

q011.explanation: Relative `delay` drifts by the loop body's execution time each cycle; `delay until Next_Release` maintains an exact period.

q012.explanation: Ravenscar (and the slightly more expressive Jorvik profile in Ada 2022) enables certified, deadlock-free, deterministic real-time systems.

q013.explanation: `Ada.Containers` provides both indefinite/definite heap containers and `Bounded_*` versions for zero-heap embedded systems.

q014.explanation: `Indefinite_*` containers hold unconstrained types like `String` or class-wide `T'Class` whose size varies per element.

q015.explanation: Ada 2012 generalized container iteration and indexing (`Vec (I)`) via language-defined aspects.

q016.explanation: `Unchecked_Conversion` is Ada's explicit bit-cast; always assert matching sizes and check `'Valid` on scalar results.

q017.explanation: Ada representation clauses specify exact byte offsets and bit ranges down to the bit level, independent of endianness guesses.

q018.explanation: `Interfaces.C` and `Import`/`Export`/`Convention` aspects make FFI with C clean and type-safe.

q019.explanation: `Atomic` and `Volatile` constrain compiler optimizations and memory access atomicity for hardware and low-level concurrency.

q020.explanation: Deriving from `Ada.Finalization.Controlled` or `Limited_Controlled` runs `Finalize` automatically when an object leaves scope.

q021.explanation: Associating an access type with a custom `Storage_Pool` (`for Ptr'Storage_Pool use Arena;`) controls where and how `new` allocates.

q022.explanation: `pragma Restrictions` enforces system-wide architectural invariants across all units at build time.

q023.explanation: Ada 2022 added parallel loops/blocks, `@` target-name shorthand, `Big_Numbers`, and `[...]` container aggregates.

q024.explanation: The `@` target-name shorthand avoids repeating long record/array expressions on the right-hand side of `:=`.

q025.explanation: Timed `select` statements prevent indefinite blocking when calling an entry on a busy or unresponsive task.

q026.explanation: ATC (`select ... then abort`) supports clean cancellation/timeouts without `pthread_cancel` hazards (disallowed in Ravenscar).

q027.explanation: Qualified names (`Pkg.Proc`), `use type` for operators, and local `renames` keep large codebases readable.

q028.explanation: `Static_Predicate` is restricted to static discrete/string sets so the compiler can check `case` exhaustiveness against it.

q029.explanation: Unhandled exceptions in a task terminate that task without propagating to its parent; production systems install `Ada.Task_Termination` handlers.

q030.explanation: Always use `Ada.Real_Time` for timeouts, watchdogs, and periodic task scheduling.

q031.explanation: Combining `-gnatwa -gnatwe -gnata` in CI catches latent bugs early.

q032.explanation: Combining `tagged`, `limited`, and `private` models non-copyable, extensible system resources cleanly.

q033.explanation: Ada's stream attributes (`'Read`, `'Write`, `'Input`, `'Output`) serialize/deserialize structured types directly.

q034.explanation: Only suppress checks on hotspots proven safe (e.g., via SPARK/GNATprove); keeping checks enabled in production prevents silent memory corruption.

q035.explanation: Ada's accessibility rules prevent storing a shorter-lived anonymous `access` parameter into a longer-lived global pointer.

q036.explanation: Bounded containers, `No_Implicit_Heap_Allocations`, and custom pools keep memory deterministic in embedded systems.

q037.explanation: GNATprove translates SPARK Ada and its contracts into verification conditions discharged by SMT provers.

q038.explanation: A parameter of specific type `T` binds statically; `T'Class` enables runtime polymorphism across all descendants of `T`.

q039.explanation: `Pure` packages are side-effect-free, have no elaboration order issues, and are safe for distributed/multi-partition Ada.

q040.explanation: `Ada.Environment_Variables.Value ("PATH")` and `Exists` provide standard OS environment access.

q041.explanation: `AUnit` and Alire test runners support structured unit and regression testing in CI.

q042.explanation: Strong nominal typing + contracts + SPARK make illegal states unrepresentable and verifiable before deployment.

q001.explanation: Elixir compiles to BEAM bytecode, inheriting Erlang/OTP's lightweight processes, preemptive scheduling, and fault tolerance.

q002.explanation: BEAM runs one scheduler per CPU core with isolated preemptive processes, trading raw numeric throughput for predictable concurrency and uptime.

q003.explanation: IEx is the interactive shell, Mix is the build/project CLI, Hex is the package registry, and Livebook provides interactive notebooks.

q004.explanation: `mix new my_app --sup` scaffolds a project including an `Application` module and root `Supervisor`.

q005.explanation: `h` displays inline documentation compiled from `@doc` and `@moduledoc` module attributes.

q006.explanation: Elixir identifies functions by `Module.name/arity`, so `greet/1` and `greet/2` are distinct functions.

q007.explanation: Public functions use `def` and private helper functions use `defp`.

q008.explanation: `a |> f(b)` desugars to `f(a, b)`, enabling readable left-to-right data transformation pipelines.

q009.explanation: `String.trim/1` strips surrounding whitespace, and `String.upcase/1` converts the string to uppercase.

q010.explanation: Elixir data is immutable (persistent structural sharing), while variables can be rebound to new values.

q011.explanation: Atoms are named constants stored in a global atom table; booleans `true`, `false`, and `nil` are also atoms.

q012.explanation: BEAM's atom table is fixed-size and not garbage-collected; use `String.to_existing_atom/1` or keep strings for untrusted input.

q013.explanation: Tuples have O(1) size and indexing; linked lists have O(1) prepend (`[h | t]`) but O(n) `length/1`.

q014.explanation: The cons operator `[head | tail]` splits a non-empty list into its first element and the remaining list.

q015.explanation: Keyword lists like `[a: 1, b: 2]` are syntactic sugar for `[{:a, 1}, {:b, 2}]`, commonly used for options.

q016.explanation: `%{map | key: val}` updates an existing key (raising `KeyError` if absent); `Map.put/3` inserts or updates.

q017.explanation: `=` is the pattern match operator: it binds variables on the left to match the structure on the right, or raises `MatchError`.

q018.explanation: `^x` prevents rebinding `x` and asserts that the matched value equals `x`'s current value.

q019.explanation: Because `^x` pins `x` to `1`, matching `2` against `1` fails with `** (MatchError) no match of right hand side value: 2`.

q020.explanation: A successful match expression returns the right-hand side value (`{:ok, 42}`) while binding pattern variables (`value = 42`).

q021.explanation: `case` matches one value, `cond` tests boolean clauses, `with` chains `<-` matches, and `if` checks a single condition.

q022.explanation: Guards only permit side-effect-free kernel BIFs/macros (`is_integer/1`, `and`, `map_size/1`, etc.), not arbitrary `Enum` functions.

q023.explanation: `==` and `!=` compare numeric values across integer/float, whereas `===` and `!==` require identical types.

q024.explanation: Strict `and`/`or`/`not` raise `BadBooleanError` on non-booleans (and work in guards); `&&`/`||`/`!` treat `nil` and `false` as falsy.

q025.explanation: Double-quoted strings are binaries (`is_binary/1`); single-quoted literals are charlists (`[104, 101, 108, 108, 111]`), used mainly for Erlang interop.

q026.explanation: `<>` concatenates binaries (`"hello" <> " world"`), while `++` concatenates lists.

q027.explanation: Only `false` and `nil` are falsy in Elixir; `0`, `""`, `[]`, and `{}` are all truthy.

q028.explanation: Sigils provide concise literals: `~r` for Regex, `~w(... )a` for atom word lists, `~s` for strings, and `~D` for `Date` structs.

q029.explanation: `/` always returns a float (`3.5`), while `div/2` performs integer division (`3`) and `rem/2` returns the remainder (`1`).

q030.explanation: Elixir uses `\\` for default argument values, which generates both `greet/1` and `greet/2`.

q031.explanation: If no `case` pattern matches, BEAM raises `CaseClauseError`; add a catch-all `_ -> ...` clause when needed.

q032.explanation: `_` matches anything without binding, and `_name` documents intent while silencing unused-variable compiler warnings.

q033.explanation: `Map.get/3` returns the default value (`0`) when the key is missing (`nil` if no default is given).

q034.explanation: Dot access `map.key` asserts the key exists (raising `KeyError` if absent), while bracket `map[:key]` uses `Access` and returns `nil`.

q035.explanation: When a `<-` match fails and no matching `else` clause handles it, `with` immediately returns the non-matching value (`{:error, :bad}`).

q036.explanation: `defstruct` inside `defmodule User` creates `%User{name: nil, role: :member}` backed by a bare map with `__struct__: User`.

q037.explanation: Structs are maps with a `__struct__` key, so both `%User{...}` and `%{...}` patterns (and `^` pinning) work; Elixir has no `instanceof`.

q038.explanation: Binary pattern matching with `<>` can match fixed-size string prefixes and bind the remaining binary.

q039.explanation: `@doc` documents the following public function (and can contain `iex>` doctests), while `@moduledoc` documents the module.

q040.explanation: `mix format` enforces consistent canonical formatting across Elixir codebases using `.formatter.exs`.

q041.explanation: `.ex` files are compiled into `.beam` artifacts during `mix compile`, while `.exs` scripts are evaluated directly in memory.

q042.explanation: Elixir is expression-oriented with top-to-bottom multi-clause function heads, while `|>` passes the left value as the *first* argument.

q001.explanation: Anonymous functions require a dot before the parentheses (`add.(2, 3)`) to distinguish them from named functions.

q002.explanation: The capture operator `&` creates compact anonymous functions (`&1`, `&2`, ...) or captures named functions (`&String.upcase/1`).

q003.explanation: Elixir closures capture immutable bindings, support multiple clauses, and are called with `.()`.

q004.explanation: Tail-recursive functions (often using an accumulator) avoid stack growth and can loop indefinitely on BEAM.

q005.explanation: `Stream` defers computation until consumed by an eager function like `Enum.take/2` or `Enum.to_list/1`, avoiding large intermediate lists.

q006.explanation: `Stream.filter` and `Stream.map` are lazy; `Enum.take(2)` pulls elements until two even squares (`4` and `16`) are produced.

q007.explanation: `for {k, v} <- list, into: %{}, do: {k, v * 2}` builds a map directly via the `Collectable` protocol.

q008.explanation: `for x <- [1, 2, 3], reduce: 0 do acc -> acc + x end` folds over items cleanly inside comprehension syntax.

q009.explanation: Protocols dispatch on data types; behaviours define module contracts; structs define structured data schemas.

q010.explanation: `@enforce_keys` ensures required struct fields are supplied whenever the `%Module{}` literal syntax is used.

q011.explanation: Tagged tuples compose cleanly with pattern matching and `with`; exceptions are reserved for unexpected failures or bang (`!`) functions.

q012.explanation: `with ... do ... else ... end` intercepts failed `<-` matches so callers receive consistent error shapes.

q013.explanation: `rescue` handles exceptions, `catch` handles `throw`/`exit`, `after` always runs cleanup, and `else` handles normal completion.

q014.explanation: Because BEAM processes are isolated and supervised, restarting a failed worker restores clean state without corrupting other requests.

q015.explanation: Bitstring integers default to big-endian unsigned: `<<0, 2>>` in 16-bit big-endian is `2`, and `rest::binary` captures `<<3, 4>>`.

q016.explanation: Appending to a list of iodata chunks is O(1) per chunk and avoids O(n^2) binary copying in templates and HTTP responses.

q017.explanation: All four directives serve distinct lexical roles: `alias` shortens names, `import` pulls functions, `require` loads macros, and `use` runs `__using__/1`.

q018.explanation: Macros receive ASTs and return ASTs built with `quote do ... unquote(expr) ... end`.

q019.explanation: Generating minimal `quote` AST that calls a standard runtime function improves stack traces, readability, and compile times.

q020.explanation: Protocols can provide a default `Any` implementation opted into via `@derive` or `@fallback_to_any true`.

q021.explanation: Compile-time config (`config.exs`) is baked into the build; `runtime.exs` reads `System.get_env/1` when the release starts.

q022.explanation: Setting `runtime: false` prevents Mix/releases from booting the dependency's OTP application when it is only a build/lint tool.

q023.explanation: `async: true` schedules the test module concurrently on BEAM schedulers, provided it does not mutate shared global state.

q024.explanation: `doctest` keeps documentation examples verified by running `iex>` expressions and asserting their printed results.

q025.explanation: Mox enforces explicit behaviour contracts and process-isolated expectations so concurrent tests never interfere.

q026.explanation: Credo lints style/design, Dialyzer performs success-typing analysis, ExUnit runs tests, and `mix format --check-formatted` gates formatting in CI.

q027.explanation: `@spec` annotations are metadata for Dialyzer and ExDoc; they do not add runtime type checks on their own.

q028.explanation: `Enum.reduce/3` folds the collection from left to right starting at `0`, summing `1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10`.

q029.explanation: `Enum.group_by/2` returns a map keyed by the classifier function's return value, with lists of matching elements.

q030.explanation: Prepending `[x | list]`, `elem/2`, and `tuple_size/1` are O(1); `length(list)` traverses the linked list in O(n).

q031.explanation: Prepending + reversing once at the end keeps list construction O(n) total instead of O(n^2).

q032.explanation: `get_in(data, [:user, :profile, :email])` safely traverses nested structures, returning `nil` if an intermediate key is `nil`.

q033.explanation: `setup` runs per-test, `setup_all` runs once per module, and `{:ok, keyword_or_map}` populates the test context regardless of `async`.

q034.explanation: `Integer.parse/1` returns `{int, rest}` or `:error` for partial/lenient parsing; `String.to_integer/1` requires the entire string to be a valid integer.

q035.explanation: Macros operate at compile time on unevaluated ASTs, allowing them to inspect or transform code structure before execution.

q036.explanation: Elixir intentionally omits `Access` from structs by default so typos fail with `KeyError` on `user.field` rather than silently returning `nil`.

q037.explanation: `File.stream!/1` produces a lazy stream that reads line-by-line without buffering the whole file in RAM.

q038.explanation: `@derive` lets libraries like `Jason` or `Inspect` generate protocol implementations for structs at compile time.

q039.explanation: `Enum.chunk_every/2` groups elements into lists of size `2`, keeping the final partial chunk `[5]` unless `:discard` is passed.

q040.explanation: `System.get_env/2` returns the fallback string `"4000"` when the environment variable is unset.

q041.explanation: `mix test --stale` uses the compile-time dependency graph to re-run only tests impacted by recent edits.

q042.explanation: Idiomatic Elixir pairs `Enum`/`Stream`, tagged tuples + `with`, and `@behaviour` + `Mox`, while avoiding unbounded dynamic atom creation.

q001.explanation: BEAM processes are lightweight, isolated, and preemptively scheduled, communicating via asynchronous message passing.

q002.explanation: Message passing in BEAM is asynchronous and copy-based (except large refc binaries > 64 bytes, which are reference-counted).

q003.explanation: Use `link` when two processes should share fate (e.g., supervisor-child), and `monitor` when you only want a `:DOWN` message on exit.

q004.explanation: Trapping exits lets supervisors or cleanup processes handle linked exits as normal messages instead of crashing immediately.

q005.explanation: Selective `receive` scans the mailbox for the first matching message and leaves non-matching messages queued.

q006.explanation: `Task.async` links to the caller (default 5s `await` timeout); `Task.Supervisor` isolates failures under a dedicated supervisor.

q007.explanation: `Task.async_stream/3` caps concurrent tasks (default `System.schedulers_online/0`) so large workloads don't overwhelm DB pools or APIs.

q008.explanation: `Agent` is a minimal abstraction over `GenServer` for holding and updating state via `Agent.get/2` and `Agent.update/2`.

q009.explanation: `handle_call` replies to `call`, `handle_cast` handles `cast`, `handle_info` handles raw messages, and `handle_continue` finishes setup without blocking `init/1`.

q010.explanation: Slow `init/1` delays the entire supervision tree startup; `handle_continue/2` runs immediately after `init/1` returns without stalling the supervisor.

q011.explanation: Every `GenServer` is a single sequential process; use `ETS`, stateless functions, or partitioned/pooled processes when high concurrency is needed.

q012.explanation: `GenServer.call` timeouts only abort the caller's wait; the request already in the mailbox is still processed by the server.

q013.explanation: `:one_for_one` isolates independent workers; `:one_for_all` couples all siblings; `:rest_for_one` models ordered dependencies.

q014.explanation: `DynamicSupervisor` starts with no initial children and spawns workers on demand via `DynamicSupervisor.start_child/2`.

q015.explanation: `:permanent` is default for long-lived services; `:transient` fits tasks that may exit `:normal`; `:temporary` never restarts.

q016.explanation: Supervisors escalate failures when a child crashes repeatedly (default 3 restarts in 5 seconds) instead of spinning forever.

q017.explanation: `mix release` creates a production-ready release artifact configured at boot by `config/runtime.exs`.

q018.explanation: Distributed Erlang/Elixir provides transparent messaging and node monitoring, not automatic distributed consensus during partitions.

q019.explanation: `:pg` tracks named groups of PIDs across connected BEAM nodes and is used by libraries like `Phoenix.PubSub`.

q020.explanation: Changesets separate untrusted external params (`cast/3`) from domain validation (`validate_required/2`, constraints) before `Repo` writes.

q021.explanation: `Ecto.Multi` builds a composable transaction pipeline so partial failures roll back cleanly and report which step failed.

q022.explanation: `Repo.preload(posts, :author)` or `from p in Post, join: a in assoc(p, :author), preload: [author: a]` fetches associations in bounded queries.

q023.explanation: Plugs are composable middleware functions or modules operating on `%Plug.Conn{}` structs.

q024.explanation: LiveView streams prune rendered items from server process state, drastically reducing memory per connected socket.

q025.explanation: Checking `if connected?(socket)` in `mount/3` prevents subscribing to PubSub or starting timers during the initial HTTP pass.

q026.explanation: ETS provides fast node-local concurrent in-memory tables owned by a process; it does not replicate across cluster nodes.

q027.explanation: `:persistent_term` gives ultra-fast zero-copy reads across processes, but writes are expensive because they trigger global GC on old terms.

q028.explanation: Per-process heaps mean short-lived request processes often exit and reclaim all memory at once without even running GC.

q029.explanation: `:telemetry` decouples event emission in libraries from metrics/logging backends like Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or LiveDashboard.

q030.explanation: NIFs share the VM address space for speed, while Ports isolate native crashes in an external OS process communicating over stdio/pipes.

q031.explanation: `Registry` is a fast, partitioned local process registry with automatic cleanup on process exit; for cluster-wide groups use `:pg` or Horde.

q032.explanation: `:via` tuples let you name dynamic processes by arbitrary terms (strings, integers) without leaking atoms.

q033.explanation: ETS tables are linked to their creating/owner process; using a long-lived supervisor/GenServer or `:heir` prevents accidental table loss.

q034.explanation: `Process.send_after/3` returns a timer reference and delivers the message asynchronously to `handle_info/2`.

q035.explanation: `PartitionSupervisor` shards traffic across N supervised workers using `{:via, PartitionSupervisor, {MySup, key}}`.

q036.explanation: OTP invokes `MyApp.Application.start(:normal, [])` when starting the `:my_app` application.

q037.explanation: `System.unique_integer([:positive, :monotonic])` is lock-free and guaranteed unique and monotonic within a VM instance.

q038.explanation: Elixir extends beyond web apps into ML/numerical computing (`Nx`) and embedded firmware (`Nerves`).

q039.explanation: Context modules keep controllers and LiveViews thin and make domain logic reusable across HTTP, LiveView, Oban jobs, and tests.

q040.explanation: BEAM exposes rich runtime introspection for diagnosing mailbox backlogs, memory growth, and supervision hierarchy in production.

q041.explanation: Sub-binaries share references to the parent refc binary (>64 bytes); calling `:binary.copy/1` detaches small slices from huge buffers.

q042.explanation: Supervision isolation, avoiding single-GenServer bottlenecks, and `runtime.exs` are core OTP practices; untrusted work belongs under `Task.Supervisor`.

q001.explanation: Odin is a data-oriented procedural language designed for clarity, explicit control over memory, and high performance without hidden exceptions or methods.

q002.explanation: Odin was created by Ginger Bill (Bill Hall) in 2016 as an alternative to C for systems and game/graphics programming.

q003.explanation: `odin run` compiles and runs, `odin build` emits a binary, `odin check` validates syntax/types only, and `odin test` executes test procedures.

q004.explanation: Odin uses `-o:none`, `-o:minimal`, `-o:size`, `-o:speed`, and `-o:aggressive` for optimization levels.

q005.explanation: `-debug` embeds debug symbols so debuggers like GDB, LLDB, or RemedyBG can inspect Odin variables and stack frames.

q006.explanation: An executable Odin program starts at `main :: proc()` inside `package main`.

q007.explanation: `x := 10` creates a mutable runtime variable, while `X :: 10` or `f :: proc()` binds an immutable compile-time constant.

q008.explanation: Odin zero-initializes all variables by default unless explicitly opted out with `---`.

q009.explanation: Assigning `---` tells the compiler not to zero-initialize the variable, which is useful for large scratch buffers.

q010.explanation: In Odin, `string` is a fat pointer `(data, len)` (UTF-8 by convention), not a null-terminated C string; `int`/`uint` are pointer-sized, `f32`/`f64` are floats, and `rune` is a Unicode code point.

q011.explanation: `distinct` creates a new type that shares the underlying representation but is not implicitly interchangeable with the base type.

q012.explanation: Untyped constants like `10` or `3.14` adapt seamlessly to compatible types (e.g., `u8`, `i64`, `f32`) without casts unless overflow occurs.

q013.explanation: When both operands are integers, `/` performs integer division and discards the fractional part; `%` yields the remainder.

q014.explanation: Odin enables runtime bounds and overflow checks in default builds; wrapping requires explicit `@(no_bounds_check)` or `-no-bounds-check`.

q015.explanation: Odin uses `&&` (logical AND), `||` (logical OR), and `!` (logical NOT), with short-circuit evaluation.

q016.explanation: In Odin, `~` is bitwise XOR (and unary bitwise NOT), `&~` clears bits, `..=` is inclusive, and `..<` is exclusive of the upper bound.

q017.explanation: `in` (and `not_in`) tests membership in maps, bit_sets, and ranges, returning a `bool`.

q018.explanation: `when` evaluates compile-time constant conditions (such as `ODIN_OS == .Linux`), discarding the untaken branch before code generation.

q019.explanation: Odin requires strict `bool` conditions and mandatory `{}` braces, while omitting outer parentheses around the condition.

q020.explanation: Odin `switch` cases break automatically at the end of each branch; `fallthrough` explicitly transfers control to the next case.

q021.explanation: Switching on an enum is checked for exhaustiveness; `#partial switch` opts out when you intentionally handle only a subset.

q022.explanation: Odin has only the `for` keyword, supporting `for i := 0; i < n; i += 1`, `for cond`, `for {}`, and `for item in slice`.

q023.explanation: In `for val, idx in collection`, the first variable is the value (or map key) and the second is the index (or map value).

q024.explanation: Labeled `break outer` and `continue outer` target a specific enclosing loop cleanly.

q025.explanation: `do` introduces a single-statement body for `if`, `when`, `for`, `switch`, and `defer` without requiring braces.

q026.explanation: `fmt.println` prints space-separated values with a trailing newline; `fmt.printfln` uses a format string with a trailing newline.

q027.explanation: Odin uses `:=`, `::`, and `: T =` for declarations; `let` is not a declaration keyword in Odin.

q028.explanation: Casting a floating-point number to an integer in Odin truncates the fractional part toward zero.

q029.explanation: `auto_cast expr` converts `expr` to the expected target type without repeating the type name, while keeping the conversion explicit in source.

q030.explanation: Odin inserts semicolons automatically at newlines after tokens that can end a statement; you only write `;` when placing statements on one line.

q031.explanation: `len(s)` is O(1) byte length, literals are UTF-8, and `string` is immutable; `s[0]` indexes a raw `u8` byte, while `for r in s` iterates `rune`s.

q032.explanation: Iterating a `string` with `for r in s` decodes UTF-8 code points into `rune` values.

q033.explanation: Backtick strings ignore escape sequences, `nil` represents empty pointers/slices/maps/procs, and `---` skips zero-initialization.

q034.explanation: Untyped integer literals default to `int`, which is pointer-sized (64-bit on 64-bit architectures).

q035.explanation: Untyped floating-point literals default to `f64` when inferred via `:=`.

q036.explanation: Odin uses `~x` for bitwise NOT (complement), while `!x` is logical NOT and `^` is used for pointers/dereferencing.

q037.explanation: Odin supports `0x` (hex), `0b` (binary), `0o` (octal), and underscores like `1_000_000` for readability.

q038.explanation: Odin omits exceptions, classes/methods, and hidden allocations, while heavily supporting compile-time constants (`::`) and `when`.

q039.explanation: `odin check` runs the front-end compiler checks quickly without linking a binary, making it ideal for editor/CI feedback.

q040.explanation: Odin `switch` supports comma-separated values, inclusive/exclusive ranges, and `case:` as the default branch, but does not use `if` guards inside `case`.

q041.explanation: Odin's sized numeric types encode signedness/float kind and exact bit width directly in their names.

q042.explanation: An `if` init statement declares variables scoped to the `if`/`else` chain, keeping the outer scope clean.

q001.explanation: Odin natively supports multiple return values, commonly used for `(value, ok)` or `(value, err)` idioms.

q002.explanation: Named return parameters are zero-initialized local variables; a bare `return` returns their current values (after `defer` runs).

q003.explanation: Odin procedure parameters are immutable values; to mutate caller state, pass a pointer `^T` (or mutate through a slice/map header).

q004.explanation: `#caller_location` automatically captures `runtime.Source_Code_Location` of the caller, powering assertion and allocation diagnostics.

q005.explanation: `defer` runs at the end of its enclosing block/scope in LIFO (last-in, first-out) order.

q006.explanation: Deferred statements execute in Last-In, First-Out (stack) order when leaving the scope.

q007.explanation: `or_return` propagates the trailing error (or `false` ok) to the caller if the current procedure has a matching trailing return type.

q008.explanation: `or_else` supplies a default value when an `(T, bool)` or `(T, Error)` expression fails.

q009.explanation: `or_break` (and `or_continue`) lets loops handle `(T, bool)`/`(T, Error)` iterations concisely without boilerplate `if !ok { break }`.

q010.explanation: Odin's `or_*` operators handle trailing `bool` (`false` = fail) or error values without exceptions.

q011.explanation: `using` promotes a struct field's members into the enclosing struct's namespace for composition without OOP inheritance.

q012.explanation: Odin structs support `#packed`, `#align(N)`, and `#raw_union` for layout control; Odin has no `class` keyword or methods.
